diadem.e: From Middle English diademe, dyademe, from Old French diademe, from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma, “band, especially worn around a tiara”), from διαδέω (diadéō, “bind around”).
diadem.g: An ornamental headband worn as a badge of royalty.

dial.e: The original meaning was 'sundial' and/or 'clock dial'; from Middle English diall, from Middle French dyal, from Latin diālis (“daily, concerning the day”), because of its use in telling the time of day, from Latin diēs (“day”).
dial.g: A graduated, circular scale over which a needle moves to show a measurement (such as speed).

diameter.e: From Old French diametre (French diamètre), from Latin diametros, from Ancient Greek διάμετρος (diámetros) (γραμμή (grammḗ)) (diametros grammē, “line measuring across”), from διά (diá, “across”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, dia- + -meter.
diameter.g: Any straight line between two points on the circumference of a circle that passes through the center of the circle; a chord that passes thro

diamond.e: From Middle English dyamaunt, from Old French diamant, from Late Latin diamās, from Latin adamās, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμᾱς (adámās, “diamond”). The printing sense is a calque of Dutch diamant, used by Dirck Voskens who first cut it around 1700; compare pearl, ruby (“size of type between pearl and nonpareil”).
diamond.g: A glimmering glass-like mineral that is an allotrope of carbon in which each atom is surrounded by four others in the form of a tetrahedron.

dictation.e: From Late Latin dictātiō, noun of action from dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō. By surface analysis, dictate + -ion.
dictation.g: Dictating, the process of speaking for someone else to write down the words.

die.e: From Middle English deyen, probably from Old Norse deyja, from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną (“to die”).
die.g: To stop living; to become dead; to undergo death.

die.e: From Middle English dee, from Old French de (Modern French dé), from Latin datum, from datus (“given”), the past participle of dō (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to lay out, to spread out”). Replaced Old English tasul, tesul (“die”), from Latin tessella (“die, cube”).
die.g: The cubical part of a pedestal; a plinth.

diet.e: From Middle English diet, dyet, diete, from Old French diete, from Medieval Latin dieta (“regimen, regulation; assembly”), from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita).
diet.g: The food and beverage a person or animal consumes.

diet.e: From Middle English dieten, dyeten, diȝeten, from Old French dïeter and Medieval Latin diētāre.
diet.g: To modify one's food and beverage intake so as to decrease or increase body weight or influence health.

differ.e: From Middle English differren, from Old French differer, from Latin differō (“carry apart, put off, defer; differ”), from dis- (“apart”) + ferō (“carry, bear”).
differ.g: Not to have the same traits or characteristics; to be unalike or distinct.

difference.e: From Middle English difference, from Old French difference, from Latin differentia (“difference”), from differēns (“different”), present participle of differre. Morphologically differ + -ence.

different.e: From Middle English different, from Old French different, from Latin differēns, present active participle of differō (“to differ”). Mostly supplanted native Old English ungelic in common usage, which lives on as unalike in Modern English.
different.g: Not the same; exhibiting a difference.

differently.e: From Middle English differently; equivalent to different + -ly.

difficult.e: From Middle English difficult (ca. 1400), a back-formation from difficulte (whence modern difficulty), from Old French difficulté, from Latin difficultas, from difficul, older form of difficilis (“hard to do, difficult”), from dis- + facilis (“easy”); see difficile. Replaced native Middle English earveþ (“difficult, hard”).
difficult.g: Hard, not easy, requiring much effort.

difficulty.e: From Middle English difficulte, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman difficulte and their etymon Latin difficultas, from difficul, older form of difficilis (“hard to do, difficult”), from dis- + facilis (“easy”); see difficile and difficult. Equivalent to dis- + facile + -ty.
difficulty.g: The state of being difficult, or hard to do.

dig.e: From Middle English diggen (“to dig”, 13th c.), an alteration of dīken, from Old English dīcian (“to dig a ditch, mound up earth”), from Proto-West Germanic *dīkōn, which see for cognates. This verb is denominal from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (“pool, puddle; dyke, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stab, dig”).
dig.g: To move hard-packed earth out of the way, especially downward to make a hole with a shovel. Or to drill, or the like, through rocks, roads,

dig.e: From African American Vernacular English; due to lack of writing of slave speech, etymology is difficult to trace, but it has been suggested that it is from Wolof dëgg, dëgga (“to understand, to appreciate”). It has also been suggested that it is from Irish dtuig, thus being a doublet of twig.

dignify.e: From Old French dignifier, from Late Latin dignificare, from dignus (“worthy”) + ficare (in comp.), facere (“to make”).
dignify.g: To invest with dignity or honour.

dignitary.g: An important or influential person, or one of high rank or position.

dignity.e: From Middle English dignyte, from Old French dignité, from Latin dignitās (“worthiness, merit, dignity, grandeur, authority, rank, office”), from dignus (“worthy, appropriate”), from Proto-Italic *degnos, from Proto-Indo-European *dḱ-nos, from *deḱ- (“to take”). In this sense, displaced native Old English weorþsċipe, which became Modern English worship.
dignity.g: The state of being dignified or worthy of esteem: elevation of mind or character.

diligence.e: Borrowed from French diligence, from Latin diligentia.
diligence.g: Steady application; industry; careful work involving long-term effort.

diligent.e: From Middle English diligent, from Old French diligent, from Latin dīligēns (“careful, attentive, diligent”), present participle of dīligō (“to love, esteem much”, literally “to choose, select”), from dī-, dis- (“apart”) + legō (“to choose”); see elect and select.
diligent.g: Performing with industrious concentration; hard-working and focused.

dill.e: From Middle English dile, from Old English dile (“dill, anise”); from Proto-Germanic *deliz, of uncertain, probably non-Indo-European origin, possibly a west European substrate.
dill.g: Anethum graveolens (the type species of the genus Anethum), a herb, the seeds of which are moderately warming, pungent, and aromatic, former
To still; to assuage; to calm; to soothe, as one in pain.

dilute.e: From Latin dīlūtus, from dīluere (“to wash away, dissolve, cause to melt, dilute”), from dī-, dis- (“away, apart”) + luere (“to wash”).
dilute.g: To make thinner by adding solvent to a solution, especially by adding water.

dim.e: From Middle English dim, dym, from Old English dim, dimm (“dim, dark, gloomy; wretched, grievous, sad, unhappy”), from Proto-West Germanic *dimm, from Proto-Germanic *dimmaz (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰem- (“to whisk, smoke; obscure”).

diminish.e: Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French diminuer, from Latin dīminuo) and minish.

dimness.e: From Middle English dymnes, dymnesse, from Old English dimnes, dymnys, dimness (“dimness, darkness, obscurity”), equivalent to dim + -ness.

dine.e: From Middle English dynen, from Old French disner (“to dine, eat the main meal of the day”), from Vulgar Latin *disiūnāre (“to eat breakfast”), from *disieiūnāre (“to break the fast”), from Late Latin, from dis- + iēiūnō (“to fast”), from Latin ieiūnus.
dine.g: To eat; to eat dinner or supper.

dinner.e: From Middle English dyner, from Old French disner (“lunch”, but originally “breakfast”), (modern French dîner), from Vulgar Latin *disiūnō, *disiūnāre from Latin dis- + iēiūnō (“to break the fast”).
dinner.g: The main meal of the day, often eaten in the evening.

dip.e: From Middle English dippen, from Old English dyppan, from Proto-West Germanic *duppjan, from Proto-Germanic *dupjaną; see *daupijaną (“to dip”).
dip.g: A lower section of a road or geological feature.

dire.g: Warning of bad consequences: ill-boding; portentous.

direct.e: Borrowed from Latin dīrēctus, perfect passive participle of dīrigō (“straighten, direct”), from dis- (“asunder, in pieces, apart, in two”) + regō (“make straight, rule”).

direction.e: From Middle English direccioun, from Old French direccion, from Latin dīrēctiō. Equivalent to direct + -ion.
direction.g: A theoretical line (physically or mentally) followed from a point of origin or towards a destination. May be relative (e.g. up, left, outbou

directive.e: From Middle French directif. The noun senses are from French directive (feminine form of the adjective).
directive.g: That which directs; serving to direct, indicate, or guide.

director.e: Borrowed from Middle French directeur and its source Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin dīrēctus. By surface analysis, direct + -or.
director.g: One who directs; the person in charge of managing a department or directorate (e.g., director of engineering), project, or production (as in

dirge.e: From Middle English dirige, from Latin dirige (“steer, direct”), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead, Dirige, Domine, deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam.
dirge.g: A mournful poem or piece of music composed or performed as a memorial to a deceased person.

dirt.e: From Middle English drit (“excrement”), from Old Norse drit (“excrement”), from Proto-Germanic *dritą, *dritō (“excrement”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreyd-, *treydʰ- (“to have diarrhea”). The word originally referred to excrement before shifting to the current sense of "soil". For a semantic parallel, see Norwegian skitt (“dirt, filth, grime, mud”).

disability.g: A condition characterised by a significant limitation in a person's physical or intellectual powers or ability.

disagree.e: From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”), from Old French desagreer, desagrëer (“to be disagreeable; to be unpleasant”) (modern French désagréer (“to displease”)); the English word is analysable as dis- + agree.
disagree.g: To fail to agree; to have a different opinion or belief.

disallow.e: From Middle English disallowen, desallowen, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman desalouer, Old French desalöer. By surface analysis, dis- + allow.

disannul.g: To annul, do away with; to cancel.

disappear.e: From Middle English disapeeren, equivalent to dis- + appear.

disappoint.e: From Middle English disapointen, disapoynten, from Middle French desapointer, desappointer (modern French désappointer). The word originally meant “to dispossess of an office”, and eventually broadened to mean “to frustrate the expectations or desires of” and “to defeat the realization or fulfillment of”.
disappoint.g: To sadden or displease (someone) by underperforming, or by not delivering something promised or hoped for.

disarm.e: From Middle English desarmen (“to divest of arms”), from Anglo-Norman desarmer.
disarm.g: To deprive of weapons; to deprive of the means of attack or defense; to render defenseless.

disarray.e: From Middle English disareyen (“to disarray”), from Middle French desarroyer, from Old French desareer, from des- (“dis-”) + areer (“to array”).
disarray.g: To throw into disorder; to break the array of.

disaster.e: From Middle French desastre, from Italian disastro, from dis- + astro (“star”), from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.
disaster.g: An unexpected natural or man-made catastrophe of substantial extent causing significant physical damage or destruction, loss of life or some

disavow.e: From dis- + avow, or from Old French desavouer.
disavow.g: To strongly and solemnly refuse to own or acknowledge; to deny responsibility for, approbation of, and the like.

disbelieve.g: To not believe; to exercise disbelief.

discern.e: From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.
discern.g: To detect with the senses, especially with the eyes.

discerner.g: One who, or that which, discerns, distinguishes, or judges.

discernment.e: From Middle French discernement, equivalent to discern + -ment.
discernment.g: The act of distinguishing between things.

discharge.e: From Middle English dischargen, from Old French deschargier (“to unload”), from Late Latin discarricāre (“unload”). By surface analysis, dis- + charge.
discharge.g: To accomplish or complete, as an obligation.

disciple.e: From Middle English disciple, discipul, from Old English discipul (“disciple, scholar”), from Latin discipulus (“pupil, learner”). Later influenced or superseded in Middle English by Old French deciple.
disciple.g: A person who learns from another, especially one who then teaches others.

discipline.e: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French descipline, from Latin disciplina (“instruction”), from discipulus (“pupil”), influenced by disco (“to learn”), from Proto-Indo-European *dek- (“(cause to) accept”).

disclose.e: From Middle English disclosen, from Middle French desclos, from Old French desclore, itself from Vulgar Latin disclaudere, from Latin dis- + claudere (“to close, shut”) or as a variant of discludo, discludere (cf. disclude). By surface analysis, dis- + close.

discomfit.e: From Middle English discomfiten, from Old French desconfit, past participle of desconfire (“to undo, to destroy”), from des- (“completely”), from Latin dis- + Old French confire (“to make”), from Latin cōnficiō (“to finish up, to destroy”), from com- (“with, together”) + faciō (“to do, to make”).
discomfit.g: To embarrass (someone) greatly; to confuse; to perplex; to disconcert.

discomfiture.e: From Old French desconfiture (“rout, defeat”); compare French déconfiture.

discomfort.e: From Middle English discomforten, from Anglo-Norman descomforter, equivalent to dis- + comfort.

disconcert.e: From Middle French desconcerter, from des- (“dis-”) + concerter (“to bring into agreement, organize”).
disconcert.g: To upset the composure of; to startle.

discontinue.e: From Old French descontinuer, equivalent to dis- + continue.
discontinue.g: To interrupt the continuance of; to put an end to, especially as regards commercial productions; to stop producing, making, or supplying.

discord.e: Circa 1230, Middle English descorde, discorde; from Anglo-Norman, Old French descort (derivative of descorder), descorde (“disagreement”); from Latin discordia, from discors (“disagreeing, disagreement”), from dis- (“apart”) + cor, cordis (“heart”). Verb derives from Middle English discorden, from Anglo-Norman, Old French descorder.
discord.g: Lack of concord, agreement, harmony; disaccord.
To untie things which are connected by a cord.

discourage.e: From Middle French descourager (modern French décourager), from Old French descouragier, from des- and corage. By surface analysis, dis- + courage.
discourage.g: To extinguish the courage of; to dishearten; to depress the spirits of; to deprive of confidence; to deject.

discourse.e: From Middle English discours, borrowed from Middle French discours (“conversation, speech”), from Latin discursus (“the act of running about”), from Latin discurrō (“run about”), from dis- (“apart”) + currō (“run”). Spelling modified by influence of Middle French cours (“course”).

discover.e: From Middle English discoveren, from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperiō, discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō.
discover.g: To find or learn something for the first time.

discovery.e: from discover + -ery, on the pattern of the pair recover, recovery.

discreet.e: From Middle English discrete, from Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, from past participle of discernere.
discreet.g: Respectful of privacy or secrecy; exercising caution in order to avoid causing embarrassment; quiet; diplomatic.

discretion.e: From Middle English discrecioun, from Old French discretion, from Late Latin discrētiō, from Latin discerno. Equivalent to discreet + -ion.

discuss.e: From Middle English discussen, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman discusser (French discuter), from Latin discussus, past participle of discutiō (“to strike or shake apart, break up, scatter; examine, discuss”), from dis- (“apart”) + quatiō (“to shake”).
discuss.g: To converse or debate concerning a particular topic.

discussion.e: From Old French discussion, from Late Latin discussiō, from Latin discutiō. By surface analysis, discuss + -ion.
discussion.g: Conversation or debate concerning a particular topic.

disdain.e: From Middle English disdeynen, from Old French desdeignier (modern French dédaigner).
disdain.g: A feeling of contempt or scorn.

disease.e: From Middle English disese, from Anglo-Norman desese, disaise, from Old French desaise, from des- + aise. By surface analysis, dis- + ease.
disease.g: An abnormal condition of a human, animal or plant that causes discomfort or dysfunction; distinct from injury insofar as the latter is usual

diseased.g: Affected with or suffering from disease.

disfigure.e: From Middle English disfiguren, from Anglo-Norman desfigurer.
disfigure.g: to irreversibly damage the shape or structure of something, negatively affecting its appearance or functionality without completely destroyi

disgrace.e: From Middle French disgracier. Mostly displaced Modern English shand.
disgrace.g: The condition of being out of favor; loss of favor, regard, or respect.

disguise.e: From Middle English disgisen, disguisen, borrowed from Old French desguiser (modern French déguiser), itself derived from des- (“dis-”) (from Latin dis-) + guise (“guise”) (from a Germanic source).
disguise.g: Material (such as clothing, makeup, a wig) used to alter one’s visual appearance in order to hide one's identity or assume another.

disgust.e: Borrowed from Middle French desgouster, from Old French desgouster (“to put off one's appetite”), from des- (“dis-”) + gouster, goster (“to taste”), from Latin gustus (“a tasting”). By surface analysis, dis- + gust (“taste”).
disgust.g: To cause an intense dislike for something.

dish.e: From Middle English dissh, disch, from Old English disċ (“plate; bowl; dish”), from Proto-West Germanic *disk (“table; dish”) (whence also Proto-Slavic *dъska, whence Bulgarian дъска́ (dăská), Polish deska, Russian доска́ (doská)), Russian чан (čan)) from Latin discus.
dish.g: A vessel such as a plate for holding or serving food, often flat with a depressed region in the middle.

dishevel.e: From Old French descheveler (modern French écheveler, ultimately from Old French chevel).

dishonest.e: From Middle English dishoneste (“dishonourable”), from Old French deshoneste, from Latin dehonestus. Equivalent to dis- + honest.

dishonestly.e: From Middle English dishonestly (“disgracefully”); equivalent to dishonest + -ly.

dishonesty.e: From Middle English dishoneste (“disgrace, filth”), from Old French deshoneste, equivalent to dis- + honesty or dishonest + -y.
dishonesty.g: The characteristic or condition of being dishonest.

dishonor.e: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honor.

dishonour.e: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honour.

disinherit.e: From Middle English disenheriten, equivalent to dis- + inherit.
disinherit.g: To exclude from inheritance; to disown.

dislodge.e: From Middle English disloggen, from Old French deslogier. Equivalent to dis- + lodge.
dislodge.g: To remove or force out from a position or dwelling previously occupied.

disloyal.e: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman desleal, desloial, equivalent to dis- + loyal.

dismantle.e: From Middle French desmanteler, itself from des- (“dis-”), mantel (“coat”) + -er (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, dis- + mantle.
dismantle.g: To take apart; to disassemble; to take to pieces.

dismay.e: From Middle English dismayen, from Anglo-Norman *desmaiier, alteration of Old French esmaier (“to frighten”), probably from Vulgar Latin *exmagare (“to deprive (someone) of strength, to disable”), from ex- + *magare (“to enable, empower”), from Proto-Germanic *maginą, *maganą (“might, power”), from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“to be able”).
dismay.g: To cause to feel apprehension; great sadness, or fear; to deprive of energy.

dismiss.e: Middle English, from Latin dimissus (“sent away, dismissed, banished”), perfect passive participle of dīmittō (“send away, dismiss”), from dis- + mittere (“to send”).
dismiss.g: To discharge; to end the employment or service of.

disobedience.e: From Middle English disobedience, dysobediaunce, from Old French desobedience. By surface analysis, dis- + obedience.

disobedient.e: From Middle English disobedient, dysobedyent, from Old French desobedient; morphologically, from dis- + obedient.

disobey.g: To refuse or (intentionally) fail to adhere to (a rule) or to obey an order from (somebody).

disorder.e: Borrowed from Middle French desordre (modern French désordre), from Old French desordre, from des- + ordre; by surface analysis, dis- + order (<< Latin ōrdō).
disorder.g: Absence of order; state of not being arranged in an orderly manner.

disorderly.e: From disorder + -ly (adjectival suffix) or from dis- + orderly.
disorderly.g: Not in order; marked by disorder or disarray.

disorderly.e: From disorder + -ly (adverbial suffix) or from dis- + orderly.
disorderly.g: In a confused or lawless manner.

dispatch.e: Borrowed from Spanish despachar and/or Italian dispacciare. Further etymology is uncertain. For first element des-, see dis-. Second element probably from either Vulgar Latin *pactāre (“to fasten"”), *pactiare or Latin -pedicāre (“to entrap, shackle”), from pedica, from pēs. Ultimately related to impeach through shared Latin root.

dispensation.e: From Middle English dispensacioun, from Old French despensacion, from Latin dispensātiō. By surface analysis, dispens(e) + -ation.
dispensation.g: The act of dispensing or dealing out; distribution

disperse.e: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

dispersion.e: From disperse + -ion, from Middle English dispersioun, from Old French dispersion, from Latin dispersiō.

displace.g: To put out of place; to disarrange.

display.e: From Middle English displayen, from Anglo-Norman despleier and Old French despleier, desploiier, from Medieval Latin displicare (“to unfold, display”), from Latin dis- (“apart”) + plicāre (“to fold”).

displease.e: English dis- + please, from Middle English displesen, from Anglo-Norman despleisir, desplere, from Old French desplere (des- + plere).
displease.g: To make not pleased; to cause a feeling of disapprobation or dislike in; to be disagreeable to; to vex slightly.

displeasing.e: Perhaps a calque of Old French desplaisant, from the verb desplere (“to displease”). By surface analysis, dis- + pleasing.

displeasure.e: From Old French desplaisir, equivalent to dis- + pleasure.
displeasure.g: A feeling of being displeased with something or someone; dissatisfaction; disapproval.

dispose.g: To eliminate or to get rid of something.

disposition.e: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō. By surface analysis, dispose + -ition.
disposition.g: The way in which something or someone is disposed or disposed of (in any sense of those terms); thus:

dispossess.e: From Middle English, from Middle French despossesser. Equivalent to dis- + possess.
dispossess.g: To deprive someone of the possession of land, especially by evicting them.

disputation.e: English dispute + -ation, from Old French disputation, from Latin disputatio.
disputation.g: The act of disputing; a dispute or argument.

dispute.e: From Middle English disputen, from Old French desputer (French disputer), from Latin disputāre (“to dispute, discuss, examine, compute, estimate”), from dis- (“apart”) + putāre (“to reckon, consider, think, originally make clean, clear up”), related to purus (“pure”).
dispute.g: An argument or disagreement; a failure to agree.

disregard.g: The act or state of deliberately not paying attention or caring about something.

dissembler.e: A modification of earlier dissimuler (from Middle English dissimulour) after resemble and semblance; equivalent to dissemble + -er.

dissension.e: From Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.
dissension.g: An act of expressing dissent, especially spoken.

dissimulation.e: From Middle English dissimulacioun, from Old French dissimulation, from Latin dissimulātiō; equivalent to dissimule + -ation.
dissimulation.g: The act of concealing the truth; hypocrisy or deception.

dissipation.e: From Middle English dissipacion, dissipacioun, from Late Latin dissipātiō. Morphologically dissipate + -ion.
dissipation.g: The act of dissipating or dispersing; a state of dispersion or separation; dispersion; waste.

dissolve.e: Recorded since c. 1374 (displacing Old English toliesan) as Middle English dissolven, from Latin dissolvere (“to loosen up, break apart”) but with the sense from Anglo-Norman dissoldre (variant of Old French dissoudre), itself from dis- (“apart”) + solvere (“to loose, loosen”). By surface analysis, dis- + solve.
dissolve.g: To terminate a union of multiple members actively, as by disbanding.

dissuade.e: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).
dissuade.g: To convince not to try or do.

distaff.e: From Middle English distaf (“distaff”), from Old English distæf (“distaff”), from *dis- (“bunch of flax”) (cognate with Middle Low German dise (“bunch of flax on a distaff”)) + stæf (“staff”) (from Proto-Germanic *stabaz (“staff, stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ-).
distaff.g: A device to which a bundle of natural fibres (often wool, flax, or cotton) is attached for temporary storage, before being drawn off gradual

distance.e: From Middle English distance, distaunce, destance (“disagreement, dispute; discrimination; armed conflict; hostility; trouble; space between two points; time interval”), from Anglo-Norman distance, distaunce, destance, Middle French distance, and Old French destance, destaunce, distaunce (“debate; difference, distinction; discord, quarrel; dispute.
distance.g: An amount of space between points (often geographical points), usually (but not necessarily) measured along a straight line.

distant.e: From Middle English distaunt, from Old French distant, from Latin distāns.

distil.e: From Late Middle English distillen (“to fall, flow, or shed in drops, drop, trickle; to shed drops; to fill (the eyes) with tears; (alchemy, medicine) to subject (something) to distillation; to obtain (something) using distillation; to distil; to condense or vaporize; (figuratively) to give (good fortune) to; to say (slanderous words)”).
distil.g: To exude (a liquid) in small drops; also, to give off (a vapour) which condenses in small drops.

distinct.e: From Middle English distincte, past participle of distincten (“to distinguish, discern”), from Old French destincter, from Latin distinctus, past participle of distinguere (“to distinguish”); see distinguish.
distinct.g: Capable of being perceived very clearly.

distinction.e: From Middle English distinccioun, from Old French distinction (attested from the 12th century), borrowed from Latin distinctiōnem, action noun of distinguō (“separate, distinguish”). By surface analysis, distinct (“to distinguish”) + -ion.
distinction.g: That which distinguishes; a single occurrence of a determining factor or feature, the fact of being divided; separation, discrimination.

distinguish.e: From Middle English distingwen, from Old French distinguer, from Latin distinguere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, set off, adorn, literally mark off”), from di-, dis- (“apart”) + stinguere, related to English stink.
distinguish.g: To recognize someone or something as different from others based on its characteristics.

distort.e: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).
distort.g: To bring something out of shape, to misshape.

distract.e: Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).

distraction.e: Borrowed from Middle French distraction, from Latin distractio. Equivalent to distract + -ion.

distraught.e: From Middle English distraught, blend of distract (“distracted”) and straught (“stretched, distraught”), past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”).
distraught.g: Deeply hurt, saddened, or worried; incapacitated by distress.

distress.e: Ultimately from Medieval Latin as if *districtiō, an assumed frequentative form of Latin distringō (“to pull asunder, stretch out”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringō (“to draw tight, strain”).
distress.g: Physical or emotional discomfort, suffering, or alarm, particularly of a more acute nature.

distribute.e: From Latin distributus, past participle of distribuere (“to divide, distribute”), from dis- (“apart”) + tribuere (“to give, impart”); see tribute.
distribute.g: To divide into portions and dispense.

distribution.e: From Old French distribution, from Latin distributio, from distribuere (“to distribute”), itself from dis- (“apart”) + tribuere (“to assign, allot”) (from tribus). By surface analysis, distribute + -ion.
distribution.g: An act of distributing or state of being distributed.

district.e: From French district, from Medieval Latin districtus (“a district within which the lord may distrain, also jurisdiction”), from Latin districtus, past participle of distringere (“to draw asunder, compel, distrain”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringere (“to draw tight, strain”).
district.g: An administrative division of an area.

disturb.e: From Middle English destourben, from Anglo-Norman distourber and Old French destorber, from Latin disturbare, intensifying for turbare (“to throw into disorder”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH-, *(s)turH- (“to rotate, swirl, twirl, move around”).
disturb.g: to confuse a quiet, constant state or a calm, continuous flow, in particular: thoughts, actions or liquids.

disturbance.e: From Middle English disturbaunce, from Old French destorbance, destourbance, from destourber (“disturb”), from Latin disturbō. By surface analysis, disturb + -ance.
disturbance.g: The act of disturbing, being disturbed.

ditch.e: From Middle English dich, from Old English dīċ (“trench, moat”) from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (compare Swedish dike, Icelandic díki, West Frisian dyk (“dam”), Dutch dijk (“dam”), German Teich (“pond”)), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, set up”) (compare Latin fīgō (“to affix, fasten”), Lithuanian diegti (“to prick.
ditch.g: A trench; a long, shallow indentation, as for irrigation or drainage.

ditch.e: From earlier deche, from Middle English dechen, from Old English dēcan (“to smear, plaster, daub”).

diverse.e: PIE word dwóh₁ The adjective is derived from Middle English divers, diverse (“different, divergent”), from Anglo-Norman divers, Anglo-Norman divers, and Old French divers (“different.

From Middle English diversen (“to differ, diverge; to become different, change; to vary; to change or vary (something); to make a distinction, distinguish; to divert”), from Anglo-Norman diverser, Middle French diverser, and Old French diverser (“to alter, change; to differ, diverge; to disagree”).

diversity.e: From Middle English diversite, from Old French diversité, from Latin dīversitās, equivalent to diverse + -ity.
diversity.g: The quality of being diverse or different; a difference or unlikeness.

divert.e: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.
divert.g: To turn aside from a course.

divide.e: From Middle English dividen, from Latin dīvidere (“to divide”).
divide.g: To split or separate (something) into two or more parts.

divided.e: From Middle English divided, devided, devidid, past participle of Middle English dividen (“to divide”), equivalent to divide + -ed.

divider.g: One who or that which divides or separates.

divination.e: From Old French divination, from Latin divinatio.
divination.g: The act of divining; a foreseeing or foretelling of future events.

divine.e: From Old French divin, from Latin dīvīnus (“of a god”), from divus (“god”).
divine.g: Of or pertaining to a god.

divine.e: Replaced Middle English devine, devin from Middle French deviner, from Latin dīvīnō.
divine.g: To foretell (something), especially by the use of divination.

diviner.e: From Middle English divinour, from Latin dīvīnātor (“diviner; fortune-teller; soothsayer”), from dīvīnāre (“to foresee, to foretell”). Equivalent to divine + -er.

division.e: From Middle English divisioun, from Old French division, from Latin dīvīsiō, dīvīsiōnem, noun of process form from perfect passive participle dīvīsus (“divided”), from dīvidō (“divide”).
division.g: The act or process of dividing anything.

divisive.g: Having a quality that divides or separates.

divorce.e: From Old French divorce, from Latin dīvortium, from dīvertere (“to turn aside”), from dī- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.
divorce.g: The legal dissolution of a marriage.

do.e: From Middle English don, from Old English dōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, do, make”). For senses 4 and 5, compare Old Norse duga, also Northern English dow. The past tense form is from Middle English didde, dude.
